extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (or advanced undergraduates) studying algebraic geometry; readers of Vakil's 'Foundations of Algebraic Geometry' / participants in Math 216
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for understanding, classifying, and constructing algebraic curves of low genus (particularly g = 0,1,2,3,4,5), their canonical embeddings, automorphisms, and key invariants (e.g., j-invariant for elliptic curves). Includes geometric constructions (plane quartics, Weierstrass cubics), complete-intersection characterizations, and moduli-dimension heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonal curves (degree-3 cover of P1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A (projective) curve over a field k admitting a degree 3 cover of P1 is called trigonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to identify trigonal curves; e.g., every non-hyperelliptic genus 3 complex curve (a plane quartic) is trigonal by projecting from any point on the quartic to P1 (choose coordinates so that the projection point is [0,0,1]). See Exercise 19.7.B for the construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperelliptic curves as double covers and degeneration limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperelliptic curves arise as double covers (central fiber) in degenerations: e.g., taking f the conic equation and g a quartic, the family f^2 + t^2 g is generically smooth quartics with t=0 a double conic; after normalization the central fiber becomes a hyperelliptic curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows hyperelliptic curves can be realized as limits of non-hyperelliptic curves; smoothness is an open condition in t and one can appeal to Bertini and generic smoothness (Theorem 25.3.3). Useful for constructing degenerations and understanding how hyperelliptic loci sit in families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automorphisms of smooth plane quartics correspond to P2 automorphisms preserving the quartic
rubrics_metrics.description: For a smooth plane quartic C' ⊂ P2 (over any field k), there is a bijection between automorphisms of C' and automorphisms of P2 that preserve C' as a set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to reduce questions about curve automorphisms to projective linear automorphisms of P2 fixing the quartic. This underlies the claim that 'most' quartics have no nontrivial automorphisms; exhibiting a specific automorphism-free quartic requires explicit checks. See Poonen's examples for constructions over arbitrary fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of genus 3 curves with no nontrivial automorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist smooth genus 3 curves (plane quartics) whose only automorphism is the identity; in characteristic 0 an explicit example is y^3 z − 3 y z^3 = 3 x^4 − 4 x^3 z + z^4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is evidence that generic quartics have trivial automorphism group. To prove for a specific curve one must show any automorphism of P2 preserving the curve is the identity (check linear transformations fixing the defining equation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical embedding criterion (non-hyperelliptic)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is a non-hyperelliptic curve of genus g, then the dualizing invertible sheaf ω_C gives a closed embedding C ↪ P^{g−1} (the canonical embedding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the hyperelliptic case ω_C gives a degree 2 map to a rational normal curve instead. Use Riemann-Roch and the genus-3 case as a guide. This embedding is called the canonical curve and is the starting point for many classification results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 4 non-hyperelliptic curves are quadric×cubic complete intersections in P3
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-hyperelliptic genus 4 curve C has canonical image in P3 of degree 6 and lies on at least one quadric Q; moreover there exists a cubic K not containing Q so that C = Q ∩ K. Conversely, any regular complete intersection of a quadric and a cubic in P3 is a canonically embedded genus 4 curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension counts: h^0(ω_C)=4, deg ω_C = 6, h^0(ω_C^{⊗2}) = 9 so there is at least one quadric vanishing on C; symmetry and B'ezout arguments show Q is irreducible and C cannot lie on two distinct quadrics. For cubics, the space has dimension ≥5, and after factoring out multiples of Q one finds a K with no common components with Q. Use Exercises 18.6.* for degree and genus checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness constraint for quadrics containing genus 4 canonical curve
rubrics_metrics.description: A genus 4 canonical curve cannot lie on two distinct irreducible quadrics Q and Q' (otherwise Q ∩ Q' would be a degree-4 curve and could not contain C of degree 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to deduce that C is cut out as Q ∩ K where K is a cubic not divisible by Q. Apply B'ezout's theorem and degree/Hilbert polynomial comparisons (Exercise 18.6.K/F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 5 canonical curves and quadrics criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-hyperelliptic genus 5 curve has canonical image of degree 8 in P4 and lies on a three-dimensional vector space of quadrics; a regular complete intersection of three quadrics in P4 is a canonically embedded genus 5 curve. Most genus 5 canonical curves are such complete intersections; the exceptions are exactly the trigonal curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Riemann-Roch counts: h^0(ω_C) = 5, h^0(ω_C^{⊗2}) = 12 so Sym^2 has dimension 15 giving at least 3 independent quadrics vanishing on C. The trigonal locus is the Zariski-closed exceptional set where the quadrics fail to cut out C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic and formula for moduli dimension: dim M_g = 3g − 3 for g > 1
rubrics_metrics.description: For g > 1, the heuristic (and classical result of Riemann) is that the moduli space of genus g curves has dimension 3g − 3; this matches low-g computations dim M2 = 3, dim M3 = 6, dim M4 = 9, dim M5 = 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: dim M_g − dim Aut(C_g) = 3g − 3 where Aut(C_g) is automorphism group dimension of a typical curve. Exceptional behavior in g = 0,1 is due to larger automorphism groups. Formally justified in stack language; heuristics via Hilbert functions and deformation theory are sketched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree 0 line bundles and the dualizing sheaf on genus 1 curves
rubrics_metrics.description: For a genus 1 curve C, deg ω_C = 0 and h^0(ω_C) = 1; the only degree 0 invertible sheaf with a nonzero section is O_C, so ω_C ≅ O_C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact underlies the structure of genus 1 curves and the identification of degree-0 line bundles with points on the curve via twists by O(p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and group law for elliptic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: An elliptic curve is a genus 1 curve E together with a choice of k-valued base point p. The set of degree-1 points (closed points) on E acquires an abelian group structure (Pic^0(E)), with p as the identity; this bijection yields the group law on points of E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the group by twisting degree-1 line bundles by O(−p) to get Pic^0; this is the canonical algebraic group structure which one can also visualize geometrically on a cubic curve via chord-and-tangent constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic curves as double covers of P1 via degree-2 line bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: For an elliptic curve E and point p, OE(2p) has 2 sections giving a degree-2 map E → P1; if char k ≠ 2 and k is algebraically closed, E has 4 branch points (one of which corresponds to 2p) and elliptic curves correspond to 4 distinct points in P1 up to automorphism (equivalently to 3 points in A1 up to affine transformations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyperelliptic Riemann-Hurwitz (Theorem 19.5.1) and Proposition 19.5.2 for uniqueness of covers branched at 4 points. The non-identity 2-torsion points correspond to the other three branch points (Exercise 19.9.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-ratio and the λ-parameter for branched 4-tuples
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ordered branch points (p,q1,q2,q3) on P1, there is a unique automorphism sending (p,q1,q2) to (∞,0,1) and q3 to λ; λ (the cross-ratio) classifies ordered 4-tuples up to projective equivalence, and the S3-action on the three nonmarked points gives six related values of λ corresponding to the same unordered elliptic curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classical parameterization of elliptic curves via the λ-line (A1 − {0,1,∞}); use Exercise 19.9.B and the six transformations listed to check equivalence. The λ parameter is the input from which the j-invariant is formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: j-invariant as a single invariant for elliptic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a single algebraic j-invariant j(λ) (explicitly j = 28 (λ^2 − λ + 1)^3 / (λ^2 (λ − 1)^2) in the text) such that j(λ) = j(λ') exactly when λ' is one of the six S3-related transforms of λ; j gives a degree-6 map P1_λ → P1_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: j classifies elliptic curves over an algebraically closed field: two genus-1 curves are isomorphic iff they have same j. The given formula is characteristic-sensitive (the 28 arises from char 2 issues); one may normalize j up to automorphisms of the j-line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass normal form (char ≠ 2,3) and j(a,b) formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If char k ≠ 2,3, an elliptic curve with a marked flex p can be written in Weierstrass normal form y^2 z = x^3 + a x^2 z + b z^3 (after coordinate changes). The j-invariant in Weierstrass coordinates is j(a,b) = 2^8·3^3 a^3 / (4 a^3 + 27 b^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate scalings and translations reduce a general cubic with a flex to this form; special characteristics require more care. The Weierstrass form makes explicit computations (torsion, flexes, group law) tractable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexes correspond to 3-torsion points
rubrics_metrics.description: Flexes of a cubic curve (points where a tangent meets the cubic with multiplicity at least 3) are exactly the 3-torsion points in the group law on E; over an algebraically closed field with char ≠ 3, there are nine flexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This geometric identification helps locate torsion structure on E; see Exercise 19.9.E for the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric chord-and-tangent group law on cubic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: On a plane cubic in Weierstrass form with origin p the point at infinity, the sum of two points q and r is obtained by: draw the line qr, let s be the third intersection with the cubic, then q + r = −s where −s is the third intersection of the line sp with the cubic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classical geometric construction realizes the abstract Pic^0 group law; associativity is not immediate from the picture but follows from identification with Pic^0 or via algebraicity proofs. Works in all characteristics provided O(3p) gives an embedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraicity of the chord-and-tangent intersection map (Proposition 19.10.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a geometrically integral cubic curve C ⊂ P2 with C_ns the smooth points, there is a unique morphism t: C_ns × C_ns → C_ns such that for distinct regular k-points p,q, t(p,q) is the third residual intersection of the line pq with C, and t(2p) is the third intersection of the tangent line at p; this construction is compatible with field extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof constructs t locally by eliminating variables (Vieta sums) and glues over affine patches; it shows the chord-and-tangent rule defines an algebraic morphism, establishing algebraicity of addition/inverse maps on the cubic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-4 and higher degree embeddings of elliptic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete linear series |O(4p)| embeds an elliptic curve E into P3 as the complete intersection of two quadrics. Higher-degree embeddings (degree 5, etc.) have more complex descriptions (e.g., degree 5 embedding as intersection of G(2,5) with linear spaces; equations given by Pfaffians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show O(4p) has sufficiently many sections and that the image lies in at least two independent quadrics which are irreducible and share no components; use B'ezout to compare degrees. Higher-degree facts require more advanced projective/Grassmannian techniques.
